etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Imperative form (命(めい)令(れい)形(けい) (meireikei)) of いらっしゃる (irassharu); shortening of いらっしゃいまし (irasshaimashi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of そ (so, “that”, medial reference marker) + れ (-re, specific pronoun referent marker).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From English cream. Doublet of クレーム (kurēmu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Related to 厚い (atsui, “thick”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 坊(ぼう) (bō) + ちゃん (-chan)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
屋(や) (ya, “building, house”) + 根(ね) (ne, “root”).
Houses in ancient Japan were dugouts, where the roof came right down to the ground.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720.
Analyzable as a compound of み (mi, see below) + 先(さき) (saki, “tip, point; promontory”).
The mi prefix is likely the honorific prefix 御(み) (mi-), and the term misaki is attested explicitly with the spelling 御(み)碕(さき) (mi-saki) in the Nihon Shoki.
Alternative theories as to the identity of the み (mi) include:
* 水(み) (mi, “water”, bound prefix form of 水(みず) (mizu)), although the semantics this suggests may instead mean “water tip”, i.e. a jutting-out of water, not of land — an inlet.
* Shift from 海(うみ) (umi, “sea”), with the same consideration as above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
た (ta-) + 平 (hira).
Attested in the Nihon Shoki (720 CE). The Ruiju Myōgishō (late Heian period) gives two readings for 平, タヒラ (tahira, modern taira) and タヒラカ (tahiraka); it is not clear whether the two had different meanings.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 忘(わす)れ (wasure, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 忘(わす)れる (wasureru)) + 物(もの) (-mono)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ut-. Cognate with Miyako 打つぃ (utsï).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from 打(う)つ (utsu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Derived from 束 (tsuka, “bunch, bundle”) + む (-mu, verb-forming suffix indicating “to look like, to seem like”).
First cited to a text from 850.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: By surface analysis, 日用(にちよう) (nichiyō, “everyday use”) + 品(ひん) (-hin, “item”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 材料 (dzoj lewᴴ, literally “materials + ingredients”). Compare modern Mandarin reading cáiliào.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 消化 (MC sjew xwaeH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with Japanese 堪(たま)る (tamaru, “to restrain oneself”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kapa/ → /kaɸa/ → /kawa/.
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kapa.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 自動(じどう) (jidō, “automatic movement”) + 車(しゃ) (-sha, “vehicle”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Literary Chinese 藝術, collectively the 六藝 (Liùyì, “Six Arts”) and 術數 (shùshù, “numerology”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First cited to the Kojiki of 712 CE and related to 苦しい (kurushii, “painful, suffering”). See that entry for more details.
-mu is an auxiliary suffix of becoming the specified state.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, in turn, from Proto-Japonic *kanto.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: First attested in 718 CE. Ultimately from Middle Chinese 角 (MC kaewk).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. From Proto-Japonic *tuno.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Appears to be a Meiji period repurposing or borrowing, probably based on written Chinese 設備 /设备 (shèbèi, “equipment; to make preparations and arrangements”) and Old Japanese 設け備ふ (makesonapu), modernized classical Japanese 設け備う (makesonau, “to arrange in preparation”).
First attested in a pocket English–Japanese dictionary from 1862, provided as the gloss for the verb season, presumably from the sense of "to make something ready".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 說 (MC sywet).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived from 掛(か)ける (kakeru, “to hang; to manipulate; to spend, invest”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Orthographic borrowing from Chinese 赤道 (chìdào).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 足(あし) (ashi, “foot”) + 跡(あと) (ato, “trace, mark”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem form”) of the verb 通る (tōru, “to go by; to go past; to go along”, intransitive).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 違(ちが)う (chigau, “to differ”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Formed from 違(ちが)う (chigau, “to differ”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 金屬 /金属 (kim dzyowk, literally “metal + be attached to; category”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *nanka.
Possibly cognate with 流れる (nagareru, “to flow”, intransitive), and 流す (nagasu, “to flow”, transitive), in reference to extending.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 欲 is a daiyōji replacing 慾
